title: Quine, Gettier and the Puzzle of Knowledge
subtitle: A three-page paper, a web of belief, and the question of what it really means to know
objectives: By the end you will be able to state the traditional analysis of knowledge as justified true belief and trace it back to Plato.
By the end you will be able to explain a Gettier case and why it threatens that analysis.
By the end you will be able to compare several responses to Gettier, including reliabilism and the knowledge-first view.
By the end you will be able to summarise Quine's attack on the two dogmas of empiricism and his image of the web of belief.
By the end you will be able to explain what naturalized epistemology is and why it is controversial.
hook:
You glance at the clock on the station wall. It says 2:15. You believe it is a quarter past two, and you are right: it really is 2:15. Your belief is true, and you had good reason for it, since station clocks are normally reliable. But unknown to you, the clock stopped exactly twelve hours ago. You happened to look at the one moment in the day when a dead clock tells the truth.

Did you *know* it was 2:15? Most people feel, instantly, that you did not. You were lucky. But notice what that intuition implies. You had a true belief, and you were justified in holding it. If that is not enough for knowledge, what is? Bertrand Russell described a version of this stopped-clock case in 1948. Fifteen years later a young American philosopher named Edmund Gettier published a paper of under three pages that turned this kind of puzzle into a crisis, and launched one of the most intense research programmes in twentieth-century philosophy. Today we follow that story, and then meet the philosopher who tried to rebuild the whole house of knowledge: W.V.O. Quine.

sections.heading: The Classic Recipe: Justified True Belief
sections.body:
**Epistemology** is the branch of philosophy that studies knowledge: what it is, how we get it, and how far it extends. You have been doing epistemology for weeks without the label, from Plato's Divided Line (Day 12) through Descartes' doubt (Day 43) to Hume's problem of induction (Day 49).

One of epistemology's central questions is simply: what *is* knowledge? Back in Plato's dialogue *Theaetetus*, Socrates and a gifted young mathematician try several answers. Knowledge is not just perception. It is not just true belief either: a skilled lawyer can persuade a jury of something true, but the jurors, who did not witness the crime, do not *know* it; they were simply talked into the right answer. Near the end, they consider the proposal that knowledge is true belief accompanied by an account (in Greek, *logos*), and even that seems to collapse. The dialogue ends, typically, in puzzlement.

By the mid-twentieth century, however, many philosophers had settled on something like Plato's last proposal, the **justified true belief** analysis, often called JTB. You know a proposition P (say, *Paris is the capital of France*) if and only if:

1. P is true.
2. You believe P.
3. You are justified in believing P.

Each condition seems necessary. You cannot know something false: you might think you know your keys are in your bag, but if they are not, you never knew it. You cannot know what you do not believe. And a lucky guess, even a true one, is not knowledge: if you pick a lottery number at random and it wins, you did not know it would. Justification, having good reasons or evidence, seems to be what turns true belief into knowledge. Put together, the three conditions seemed to be jointly sufficient as well. That neat recipe was the target of Gettier's paper.

sections.heading: Three Pages That Shook Epistemology
sections.body:
In 1963 Edmund Gettier, then a young philosopher at Wayne State University in Detroit, published “Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?” in the journal *Analysis*. Colleagues reportedly urged him to publish something to help his case for tenure, and he produced this tiny paper. It may be the most efficient piece of philosophy ever written, and he published almost nothing else in his long career.

Here is his first case, slightly simplified. Smith and Jones have both applied for the same job. Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get it (the company president told him so), and he has counted the coins in Jones's pocket: ten. So Smith believes: *Jones will get the job, and Jones has ten coins in his pocket.* From this he infers: *The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket.* That belief is justified, because it follows from a well-supported one.

But surprise: Smith, not Jones, gets the job. And, unknown to Smith, he himself happens to have ten coins in his own pocket. So his belief that the man who gets the job has ten coins in his pocket is true. It is justified. He believes it. Yet clearly he does not *know* it. It is true only because of a coincidence that has nothing to do with his reasons.

Gettier's second case: Smith has good evidence that Jones owns a Ford. He then forms, by simple logic, the belief *Either Jones owns a Ford, or Brown is in Barcelona*, having no idea where Brown is. It turns out Jones does not own a Ford at all (he was driving a rental), but by pure chance Brown *is* in Barcelona. Justified, true, believed, and not knowledge.

These are now called **Gettier cases**: situations in which someone has a justified true belief that is true only by luck. The stopped clock is one. So is a much older example: the eighth-century Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara described a desert traveller who sees a mirage of water and believes there is water ahead; when he arrives, there really is water, hidden under a rock. Scholars now cite Dharmottara as evidence that the problem was noticed in Indian epistemology over a thousand years before Gettier.

sections.heading: The Search for a Fourth Condition
sections.body:
The reaction was explosive. For decades philosophers proposed repairs, and others built ever more ingenious counterexamples to the repairs. Here are the main strategies.

**No false lemmas.** In Gettier's own cases, Smith reasons from a false belief (that Jones will get the job; that Jones owns a Ford). So perhaps knowledge is justified true belief not inferred from any falsehood. Unfortunately, cases soon appeared with no false step at all. Imagine driving through a district where, unknown to you, the locals have put up dozens of papier-mâché barn facades that look perfect from the road. You look at the one real barn and think *that's a barn*. Your belief is true and justified, and you inferred nothing false. Yet most people judge you do not know, since you would have believed the same of any fake. This is the famous **fake barn case**, published by Alvin Goldman in 1976, who credited it to Carl Ginet.

**Causal and reliabilist theories.** Goldman proposed that what matters is how a belief is produced. In his later **reliabilism**, a belief is justified if it comes from a reliable process, one that tends to produce true beliefs, such as good eyesight in good light, careful memory or sound reasoning. This shifts focus from the reasons you can cite to the processes that actually generated your belief, a move called **externalism**, since the justifying factors can lie outside your awareness. Critics ask: what if a process is reliable but you have no idea that it is, like a person who has a perfectly accurate, unexplained hunch about the future?

**Sensitivity and safety.** Robert Nozick (1981) said knowledge must *track* the truth: if P were false, you would not believe it. Others, like Ernest Sosa and Timothy Williamson, proposed **safety**: your belief could not easily have been false. The stopped clock fails both tests: had the time been different, you would still have believed 2:15.

**Knowledge first.** Finally, Williamson's *Knowledge and Its Limits* (2000) suggested the whole project was backwards. Knowledge cannot be analysed into simpler parts; it is the basic notion, and belief and justification should be understood in terms of it. This echoes Wittgenstein's family-resemblance worry (Day 73): maybe some concepts simply resist neat definitions. After sixty years there is still no agreed solution. Even so, almost everyone agrees Gettier was right that justified true belief is not enough.

sections.heading: Quine and the Two Dogmas
sections.body:
While some philosophers dissected knowledge one belief at a time, Willard Van Orman Quine (1908–2000) looked at knowledge as a whole. Quine spent nearly his whole career at Harvard. As a young man he visited the Vienna Circle (Day 71) and admired Rudolf Carnap enormously. Then he turned on their central doctrines.

In “Two Dogmas of Empiricism” (1951), perhaps the most influential philosophy paper of the century, Quine attacked two assumptions shared by the logical positivists.

The first dogma is the sharp **analytic/synthetic distinction**. Remember from Hume and Kant (Days 49 and 55) that analytic statements are supposed to be true purely by meaning (*all bachelors are unmarried*), while synthetic statements are true because of how the world is (*some bachelors are bald*). The positivists leaned heavily on this line: logic and mathematics were analytic, science synthetic and verified by experience. Quine argued that every attempt to define analyticity goes in a circle. We say *bachelor* and *unmarried man* are synonyms. But what is synonymy? Interchangeability without changing truth, or being true by definition, or by meaning... and every one of those notions quietly presupposes analyticity again. Quine concluded that the distinction is a dogma, not a discovery.

The second dogma is **reductionism**: the idea that each meaningful statement can be tested individually against experience, as the verification principle demanded. Quine replied with one of the century's most famous sentences: our statements about the external world face the tribunal of sense experience not individually but only as a corporate body. A single hypothesis never meets the world alone. It always comes bundled with background assumptions about instruments, other laws, and logic itself. When an experiment fails, logic does not tell you which belief to give up. (The French physicist Pierre Duhem had made a similar point about physics, so this is often called the **Duhem–Quine thesis**.) This is bad news for Popper's simple falsification too (Day 72): a failed prediction refutes the whole bundle, not one particular claim.

sections.heading: The Web of Belief and Neurath's Boat
sections.body:
Instead of a building with foundations, Quine pictured knowledge as a **web of belief**. At the edges, touching experience, are observation reports: *the meter reads 7*. Further in are scientific theories, and at the centre are the most general principles, mathematics and logic. When experience conflicts with the web, we must adjust somewhere. Usually we revise near the edge (perhaps the meter was faulty). But nothing is immune. Quine provocatively said that any statement can be held true come what may if we make drastic enough adjustments elsewhere, and conversely no statement is immune to revision, not even the laws of logic. He pointed out that some had proposed revising logic itself to deal with quantum mechanics.

This is a form of **holism**, the view that beliefs are confirmed or refuted only as wholes. And it means there is no sharp line between philosophy and science, or between necessary truths and empirical ones. The differences are of degree: how central a belief is, how much else would have to change if we gave it up.

Quine loved an image from Otto Neurath, a member of the Vienna Circle: we are like sailors who must rebuild their ship on the open sea, never able to dock it and reconstruct it from the best materials. Quine used it as the epigraph to his book *Word and Object* (1960). There is no dry land of certainty from which to start, which is exactly what Descartes had hoped for on Day 43.

sections.heading: Epistemology Naturalized
sections.body:
If there is no foundation outside science, where does that leave epistemology? In “Epistemology Naturalized” (1969), Quine answered: inside science. The traditional dream, from Descartes to Carnap, was to justify science from some prior, purer standpoint. Quine thought that dream had failed. Hume showed we cannot deduce general truths from experience; the positivists failed to translate science into sense-data.

So, Quine proposed, epistemology should become a chapter of psychology. Instead of asking how we *ought* to get from sense experience to theory, we should study empirically how human beings *actually* do it: how meagre input at the sense organs, light hitting the retina, sound waves striking the eardrum, produces our torrential output of theories about the world. This is **naturalized epistemology**.

It was enormously influential. Today's epistemologists draw on cognitive science, the psychology of reasoning, the study of perception and even evolutionary biology. Goldman's reliabilism is naturalistic in spirit: whether a belief-forming process is reliable is an empirical question.

The main objection is that Quine changed the subject. Epistemology is **normative**: it asks what we *should* believe, what counts as good evidence. Psychology is **descriptive**: it tells us what people *do* believe and why, including all their biases. If epistemology becomes psychology, the critic Jaegwon Kim argued in 1988, it loses its claim to say when beliefs are justified. Defenders reply that norms can be grounded in facts about which methods succeed, much as medicine grounds advice about health in biology. That debate about whether values can be read off facts should remind you of Hume's is–ought gap from Day 50.

keyQuote.text: Our statements about the external world face the tribunal of sense experience not individually but only as a corporate body.

modernConnection.title: Right for the Wrong Reasons: Gettier and Machine Learning
modernConnection.body:
Gettier cases sound like parlour games, but engineers building artificial intelligence meet them constantly. A machine-learning model can give the right answer for the wrong reason, and that is the stopped clock in silicon.

A well-known demonstration came in a 2016 paper by Marco Ribeiro and colleagues. They deliberately trained an image classifier to distinguish huskies from wolves using pictures in which the wolves usually had snow in the background. The classifier performed well, but when the researchers examined what it was attending to, it had largely learned to detect snow. Its true answers about wolves were, in Gettier's sense, lucky: justified by a pattern that happened to correlate with the truth in that data. Show it a husky in snow and it fails. Medical AI researchers have reported similar problems, for instance models that picked up on hospital-specific markings on X-ray images rather than on signs of disease itself.

Epistemologists would say these systems lack **safety**: their outputs could easily have been false. A reliabilist would ask whether the process is reliable across the situations we care about, not just in the test set. This is exactly why AI researchers now emphasise interpretability (seeing why a model answers as it does) and robustness (testing it in new conditions).

Quine is relevant too. When a model fails, engineers face the Duhem–Quine problem: was it the data, the architecture, the training procedure, the test, or the assumption about what the task even is? No failed prediction tells you which part of the web to revise.

The analogy has limits. A classifier does not *believe* anything in the way Smith does, so strictly it cannot have Gettiered knowledge. But the lesson carries over to human beings too: a true answer is not enough. We should care whether it is true for the right reasons.

vocabulary.definition: The branch of philosophy that studies knowledge, justification and rational belief.
vocabulary.example: Asking whether you can know anything about the future from past experience is a question in epistemology.

vocabulary.definition: The traditional analysis of knowledge: you know P if P is true, you believe P, and you are justified in believing P.
vocabulary.example: On the justified true belief view, your well-supported and correct belief that the shop opens at nine counts as knowledge.

vocabulary.definition: A scenario in which someone has a justified true belief that is true only by luck, and so seems not to be knowledge.
vocabulary.example: Correctly reading the time from a clock that stopped exactly twelve hours ago is a Gettier case.

vocabulary.definition: The view that a belief is justified, or counts as knowledge, when it is produced by a process that reliably yields true beliefs.
vocabulary.example: A reliabilist would say your belief that a friend is at the door is justified because your hearing in a quiet house is reliable.

vocabulary.definition: The distinction between statements true by virtue of meaning alone and statements true because of how the world is; Quine argued it could not be drawn sharply.
vocabulary.example: “Triangles have three sides” was the textbook analytic truth; “Triangles are drawn on this board” is synthetic.

vocabulary.definition: The view that beliefs or statements are confirmed or refuted not one by one but as parts of a larger whole.
vocabulary.example: When an experiment fails, holism says you could revise the theory, the instrument readings or the background assumptions.

vocabulary.definition: Quine's image of knowledge as an interconnected network, with observation at the edges and logic and mathematics at the centre, all in principle revisable.
vocabulary.example: Learning that your thermometer is broken changes a strand at the edge of your web of belief without disturbing your physics.

vocabulary.definition: Quine's proposal that epistemology should be continuous with natural science, studying empirically how humans actually form beliefs.
vocabulary.example: Research on how the brain constructs a 3D world from flat retinal images is naturalized epistemology at work.

thinkingExercise.title: Build Your Own Gettier Case
thinkingExercise.prompt: The best way to understand a Gettier case is to invent one, and then test whether any repair to the definition of knowledge survives it.
steps: Write a short story from everyday life in which someone has a belief that is true, well justified, and yet true only by luck. Check that all three JTB conditions are met.
Ask two or three people (or yourself, honestly) whether the person knows. Note the reactions.
Test the no false lemmas repair: does the person in your story reason from any false belief? Can you rewrite the story so that they do not?
Test the safety condition: could the belief easily have been false? Does this explain the intuition that it is not knowledge?
Finish with a paragraph: do you think knowledge can be given a precise definition at all, or is Williamson right that it is basic?

summary: The traditional analysis says knowledge is justified true belief, an idea foreshadowed in Plato's *Theaetetus*.
Edmund Gettier's 1963 paper showed, with cases of lucky justified true belief, that the three conditions are not sufficient; Dharmottara and Russell had noticed similar cases earlier.
Responses include no false lemmas, reliabilism, sensitivity and safety conditions, and Williamson's knowledge-first view; none has won consensus.
Quine's “Two Dogmas of Empiricism” (1951) attacked the analytic/synthetic distinction and the idea that statements can be tested one at a time.
Quine pictured knowledge as a revisable web of belief, like Neurath's boat rebuilt at sea, and proposed naturalizing epistemology as part of psychology, which critics say loses its normative force.

quiz.question: Which three conditions make up the traditional analysis of knowledge?
quiz.explanation: The justified true belief (JTB) analysis requires that P be true, that you believe it, and that you are justified in believing it.

quiz.question: In Gettier's first case, why does Smith's belief that the man who gets the job has ten coins in his pocket fail to be knowledge?
options: Because Smith had no evidence at all
Because Smith does not really believe it
Because it is true only by a coincidence unrelated to his reasons
quiz.explanation: The belief is true, justified and believed, but true only because Smith himself happens to get the job and to have ten coins, which his evidence was not about.

quiz.question: The problem raised by Gettier cases had no precedent before 1963.
quiz.explanation: The eighth-century Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara described a similar mirage case, and Bertrand Russell described the stopped clock in 1948.

quiz.question: The fake barn case was designed especially to challenge which proposed repair to the JTB analysis?
quiz.explanation: In the fake barn case the person infers nothing from a false belief, yet still seems not to know, so ruling out false lemmas is not enough.

quiz.question: According to reliabilism, what makes a belief justified?
options: Being able to state a valid argument for it
Being produced by a process that tends to produce true beliefs
quiz.explanation: Reliabilism focuses on the belief-forming process, such as good vision or memory, rather than the reasons you can cite.

quiz.question: What did Quine mean by saying statements face the tribunal of experience “only as a corporate body”?
options: Only scientific institutions can test theories
Individual hypotheses are always tested together with many background assumptions
Every statement can be verified on its own
quiz.explanation: Quine's holism holds that a failed prediction refutes a bundle of beliefs, not a single isolated statement.

quiz.question: Quine held that even the laws of logic are, in principle, open to revision.
quiz.explanation: In his web of belief, logic sits at the centre and is very rarely revised, but no statement is immune to revision.

quiz.question: An AI system identifies wolves correctly in test photos, but only because it learned to detect snow in the background. Which idea from today's lesson does this best illustrate?
options: A Gettier-style success: right answer for the wrong reason
quiz.explanation: Its answers are true but owe their truth to a lucky correlation, mirroring the luck in Gettier cases, though strictly a classifier does not have beliefs.

quiz.question: What is the main objection to Quine's naturalized epistemology?
options: It relies too heavily on God
It assumes a sharp analytic/synthetic distinction
It replaces the normative question of what we should believe with a descriptive one
quiz.explanation: Critics such as Jaegwon Kim argued that turning epistemology into psychology loses its job of telling us when beliefs are justified.

quiz.question: Neurath's image of sailors rebuilding their ship at sea expresses the idea that there is no firm foundation outside our system of beliefs from which to rebuild knowledge.
quiz.explanation: Quine used the image to reject Descartes' hope for a foundation of certainty; we must revise our beliefs while relying on them.

goDeeper.body:
One fascinating twist in the Gettier literature is **experimental philosophy**. Philosophers had assumed that everyone shares the intuition that Gettier subjects lack knowledge. In 2001 Jonathan Weinberg, Shaun Nichols and Stephen Stich published a study suggesting that intuitions about Gettier cases differed across cultural groups. If intuitions vary, can they really serve as evidence about the nature of knowledge? Later, larger studies, including a 2017 cross-cultural project led by Edouard Machery covering countries such as Brazil, India, Japan and the United States, found the Gettier intuition to be surprisingly robust and widespread. That itself is philosophically interesting: perhaps there is a shared human concept of knowledge after all.

A second route goes through **virtue epistemology**. Ernest Sosa and Linda Zagzebski proposed treating knowledge as a kind of achievement, like an archer's shot that hits the target *because* of the archer's skill rather than a lucky gust of wind. In a Gettier case, the belief is true, and it is competent, but it is not true *because* it is competent. Sosa's analysis of an apt belief, one that is accurate because adroit, borrows Aristotle's idea of virtue as excellence (Day 20) and applies it to the mind.

Finally, Quine's attack on analyticity remains contested. H.P. Grice and P.F. Strawson replied in “In Defense of a Dogma” (1956) that a distinction people can draw consistently in practice cannot be empty just because it resists definition, an argument with a Wittgensteinian flavour. And Carnap himself never accepted that Quine had refuted him.

readings.title: Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?
readings.author: Edmund Gettier
readings.note: Three pages long, in *Analysis* (1963), and very readable; there is no better primary source to start with.

readings.title: From a Logical Point of View
readings.author: W.V.O. Quine
readings.note: Contains “Two Dogmas of Empiricism”; the final section on the web of belief is the most accessible part.

readings.title: Theaetetus
readings.author: Plato
readings.note: The original investigation of what knowledge is; the closing discussion of true belief with an account sets up the whole debate.

readings.title: Epistemology: A Contemporary Introduction to the Theory of Knowledge
readings.author: Robert Audi
readings.note: A clear textbook treatment of Gettier, reliabilism and foundationalism versus coherentism.

questions: Does it matter, practically, whether a true belief counts as knowledge, as long as it is true and justified?
If Quine is right that no belief is immune from revision, could we ever discover that 2 + 2 = 4 is false? What would that even look like?
Should epistemology tell us how we ought to reason, or only describe how we do? Can it do both?
